fields.h1: What Is the Great Commission — and Does It Apply to Me?
fields.meta_title: What Is the Great Commission — and Does It Apply to Me?
fields.description: Jesus' last command was to make disciples of all nations. Here is what the Great Commission is, what it means, and why it is a task for every Christian — not just missionaries.
fields.body_html:
Before he returned to heaven, Jesus gave his followers one great marching order — a command so important the church has called it the Great Commission ever since. And though we often file it away as a job for missionaries and pastors, Jesus gave it to all his disciples, which means he gave it to you. So what exactly is the Great Commission, what does it ask, and does it really apply to an ordinary Christian with an ordinary life?

Here is what Jesus commanded, why it matters, and how every believer has a part in it.

The command itself

The best-known form comes at the end of Matthew’s Gospel: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:18–20). Notice the shape of it: a command bracketed by two staggering promises. It opens with Christ’s authority — all of it, everywhere — and closes with his presence — always, to the very end. The task is enormous, but it is framed by the King who has all power and who goes with us into it.

Mark records it more briefly: “Go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation” (Mark 16:15). And Jesus repeated the theme as he ascended: “you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth” (Acts 1:8). The scope could not be wider: all nations, the whole world, the ends of the earth.

What “make disciples” actually means

The heart of the command is not merely to win converts but to make disciples — to help people become lifelong followers and learners of Jesus. Matthew unpacks it with two participles: baptizing (bringing people to faith and into the visible family of God) and teaching them to observe all that I have commanded (helping them grow into obedient maturity). Evangelism gets a person started; disciple-making walks with them all the way. The goal is not a decision but a transformed life, and then that life helping to transform others.

Does it apply to ordinary Christians?

Here is where many quietly excuse themselves: surely this is for the specially called. But the New Testament knows no such division. Jesus gave the commission to his gathered followers, not to a professional class, and the earliest church took it as everyone’s work: when persecution scattered ordinary believers, “those who were scattered went about preaching the word” (Acts 8:4) — not the apostles, who stayed, but the ordinary members. Every Christian is sent: “As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you” (John 20:21). Every Christian is an ambassador: “we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us” (2 Corinthians 5:20).

This does not mean every believer must move overseas. It means every believer is a witness where they already are — in a family, a workplace, a neighborhood, a friendship — and a sender and supporter of those who do go far. The Great Commission is not a burden for the few; it is the shared privilege of the whole church, each in the place and role God has given.

“But I’m not gifted at this”

Perhaps the most common reason Christians hold back is a quiet sense of inadequacy: I wouldn’t know what to say; I’m not a preacher; I’m afraid. This is worth answering directly, because it stops so many. First, notice that the commission is bracketed by Christ’s authority and presence precisely so that our inadequacy is not the deciding factor — “I am with you always” is spoken to nervous, ordinary disciples. Second, God has never required eloquence, only faithfulness and love. The most powerful witness is often not a polished argument but an ordinary believer honestly telling what Christ has done for them, as the healed man simply said, “one thing I know, that though I was blind, now I see.” Third, we do not go in our own strength at all: Jesus tied the commission to the coming of the Spirit — “you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses” (Acts 1:8). The power is his; the availability is ours. You do not have to be gifted; you have to be willing, and to trust the God who works through willing, ordinary people.

Why it matters so much

Why did Jesus make this the church’s central task? Because people genuinely cannot be saved without hearing. Paul reasons it out: “How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching?” (Romans 10:14). The gospel is the one message that rescues, and it travels on human voices. If those who have it stay silent, those who need it stay lost. That is why Jesus looked at the crowds with compassion and said, “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest” (Matthew 9:37–38).

And there is a glorious end in view. The Great Commission is not a hopeless slog but a task with a guaranteed outcome: John saw it finished — “a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne” (Revelation 7:9). Christ will have his worshipers from every people on earth. When we obey the commission, we are not gambling on a lost cause; we are joining a mission the King has already promised to complete.

The great examples

Church history is lit up by ordinary people who took this command personally. Hudson Taylor left everything for inland China because he could not shake the thought of millions who had never once heard the name of Christ, and in A Retrospect he tells the story of a life poured out on the strength of Jesus’ promise to be with him always. David Brainerd spent his short life among Native Americans, his Diary recording a man who counted his own comfort as nothing beside the salvation of others. Amy Carmichael gave decades in India rescuing children, refusing in Things as They Are to soften the hard realities for comfortable supporters back home. None of them were extraordinary at the start. They were ordinary believers who took an ordinary Christian’s commission with extraordinary seriousness.

Your part in it

So what does obedience look like for you? It begins with seeing yourself as sent — a witness wherever you already are. Then, practically:

  • Pray. Jesus’ own first instruction about the harvest was to pray for laborers (Matthew 9:38). Pray for the lost you know by name, and for the spread of the gospel to the ends of the earth.
  • Speak. Look for the people God has placed around you who do not know Christ, and prayerfully, kindly, tell them — make disciples in your own circles.
  • Send and support. Not everyone goes, but everyone can send — giving to, praying for, and encouraging those who carry the gospel where you cannot.
  • Go, if he calls. For some, obedience will mean their own version of Taylor’s or Carmichael’s road. Hold your life open, and ask.

The Great Commission is Jesus’ last and greatest command, and it is not addressed to someone else. It comes with all his authority behind it and all his presence within it — “I am with you always.” You do not go alone, and you do not go in vain. The question is not whether the commission applies to you, but where, in your own life, you will begin to obey it.

Perhaps the best place to begin is simply to ask God to give you his heart for the people around you who do not yet know him — and to open your eyes to the part he has for you. For some that will be a lifelong friend patiently loved toward Christ; for others a neighbor, a coworker, a family member; for a few, a road that leads to the ends of the earth. But for every believer there is a part, and the same Lord who commissions also equips and accompanies. The church has never advanced by the efforts of a gifted few, but by ordinary Christians who believed that the risen King really does have all authority, that he really is with them always, and that his mission really will be completed — and who, believing it, opened their mouths and their lives. That invitation — to join the King’s unstoppable mission, right where you are — stands open to you today. You need not cross an ocean to begin; you need only start where God has already placed you, with the people already in front of you, and go from there.
